summary: State a1402b6d61e02217 (source level) is 1.23x faster than amdclang's build (240 pairs, CI 1.226 to 1.233; 0.0897 ms vs 0.1101 ms); static check and 77/77 battery cases pass. It launches cdiv(N,4) workgroups of 1024 threads, 4 columns per workgroup: each thread reads 16-byte chunks (global_load_dwordx4) of x and of the 4 columns at stride 4096 floats, two strides (2 x loads + 8 A loads) in flight, the x loads shared by the 4 columns, and a two-level LDS reduction with 2 barriers replaces the 9-barrier tree. Summation order differs from the baseline (within the manifest tolerance, not bit-identical). The 1.5x target was not reached. Case: the reference headroom of 1.69 is misleading; A is read exactly once (x is re-read per column but is 32 KB and cached), and a probe that makes every workgroup read the same cached column runs in 22.6 us, so 67 of the 89 us are DRAM reads of A at about 4 TB/s. Five different geometries land within 88 to 93 us, the same read plateau the rb_gemvn and mo_reduce_sum sessions hit (about 3 TB/s including launch).

friction: reference_headroom (1.69) and memory_floor_ms (0.0651) promised 1.5x, but the floor is built from the copy rate (5.95 TB/s counting read + written bytes) and read_only_tb_per_s 7.5 comes from the MFMA GEMM operand loads (agc/arch/gfx950.yaml:55), which re-read cached operands. For a kernel that only reads 268 MB from DRAM, three sessions (rb_gemvn 100 us, mo_reduce_sum 84 us, this one 89 us) plateau near 3 TB/s including launch. A measured read-only streaming rate (a reduce over 2^26 floats) in the arch file would give an honest floor for read-only kernels.

source(): the `defines` sweep still needs the whole text resent for each point, because the launch grid depends on the define (cdiv(N, NC)). I resent the same 110-line source five times. A source(sha, defines, launch) form, or launch expressions that can reference the defines, would make the sweep one-liners.

Defining NB through `defines` broke the build: bench/llm/rocblas_common.h uses NB as a template parameter name (lines 43, 96, 113). The error was clear, but a note on reserved names in that header would save a round trip.

No diagnostic separates DRAM read rate from wave dispatch other than hand-editing the address computation for a probe (0298130f26b9e3fe: s_mul of col * lda replaced by 0). A built-in 'same code, all workgroups on workgroup 0's data' probe would give the non-memory time in one call.

9fd9a56980fc23d9 (33 KB LDS per 1024-thread workgroup) was 14 % slower than the 16 KB variant; I did not call features on it, so whether LDS limited its occupancy is a guess. check() could return the occupancy limiter alongside lds_bytes.

No page-size or TLB information for the buffers, and no count of concurrently running waves: I could not tell whether the 4 TB/s read plateau is bandwidth, TLB misses (268 MB, columns 32 KB apart) or the SR-IOV VF.
lessons: rb_gemvt (column-major A^T x, 8192x8192, 268 MB read once): the rocBLAS source reads one float per thread per wait (32 iterations) and reduces with a 9-barrier LDS tree, at 0.110 ms. Rewriting to float4 per thread with all loads in flight and a 2-level LDS reduction gave only 1.19x to 1.23x, because the kernel then sits on the DRAM read plateau.

Cached-column probe: making every workgroup read column 0 dropped the kernel from 0.0906 ms to 0.0226 ms (unpaired). So launch of 8192 workgroups x 4 waves, the arithmetic, the LDS reduction and the x reads together cost about 22 us, and reading 268 MB of A costs about 67 us (about 4 TB/s). This edit (replace the col * lda multiply by 0) is a cheap way to split memory time from everything else.

Geometry did not matter at the plateau: 8192 WG x 4 waves 90.6 us, 4096 WG x 4 waves with 2 columns sharing x loads 88.8 us, 8192 WG x 16 waves 92.6 us, 2048 WG x 16 waves with 4 columns 89.0 us (candidate times from separate 60-pair runs; the 2-column and 4-column variants are parity in a 240-pair compare, 1.0036). One wave per column (block 64, 16 load pairs in flight) was slower at 98.4 us.
Removing both barriers of the 2-level reduction changed nothing (0.0946 ms unpaired against 0.0906 ms paired for the parent): once the tree is two levels, barriers are not on the critical path.
Sharing the x loads between 2 or 4 columns of a workgroup (halving or quartering the cached x reads) gained nothing measurable: cached re-reads of a 32 KB vector are free next to the DRAM stream.

8 columns per 1024-thread workgroup with per-column LDS arrays (33 KB LDS) was 14 % slower than 4 columns (16 KB LDS): 0.1037 ms against 0.0890 ms in a direct compare. The cause was not checked (LDS occupancy is my guess).

The bench headroom figure overstates what a read-only kernel can gain: reference headroom 1.69 here, yet the best state stays at headroom 1.38, matching rb_gemvn (1.54) and mo_reduce_sum (1.30). Treat about 85 to 90 us for 268 MB read once as the practical floor on this device until a read-only rate is measured.

session.final:
`rb_gemvt` reached **1.23x** over amdclang's build, not the 1.5x target (0.0897 ms against 0.1101 ms; 240 pairs, CI 1.226–1.233). The state to ship is `a1402b6d61e02217`; it passes the static check and all 77 battery cases, and the report is filed.

**What changed (source level only):**
- Each thread reads 16-byte chunks with wide loads instead of one float per wait.
- A workgroup of 1024 threads handles 4 columns, sharing the `x` loads between them, with all loads issued before the first wait.
- A two-level LDS reduction with 2 barriers replaces the 9-barrier tree.
- The summation order differs from the baseline, so results match within the manifest tolerance, not bit for bit.

**Which case this is:** the kernel is bound by reading `A` from memory, and the reference headroom of 1.69 overstates what is available. `A` is read exactly once; `x` is re-read per column but is 32 KB and cached. A probe that made every workgroup read the same cached column ran in 22.6 µs, so about 67 of the 89 µs are reads of `A` at roughly 4 TB/s. The `rb_gemvn` and `mo_reduce_sum` sessions stopped at a similar level (100 µs and 84 µs).

Removing both barriers in a probe changed nothing, so the reduction is not on the critical path.

I stopped after six timed candidates and two probes, well short of the budget, because block size, columns per workgroup and barrier removal each brought under 1 %. No machine-IR edits were attempted: the block-1024 variant already runs a single loop
